title: Value Indicator: "When Am I Ever Going to Use This?"
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart uses a familiar classroom flashpoint — a student groaning "When am I ever going to use this?" — as a diagnostic prompt for his Five Key Beliefs framework from The Will to Learn. He argues the complaint is really two signals at once: a culturally inherited utilitarian bias that treats usefulness as the only measure of worth, and a more immediate sign that the student's will is being repelled by the task. Rather than treating every such complaint as a Value problem by default, he walks through how the same surface complaint can trace back to a Credibility, Effort, Efficacy, or Belonging deficit instead, each requiring its own fix. Only after ruling those out does he treat it as a genuine Value issue, addressed through Mini-Sermons, Feasts of Knowledge, and Valued Within methods. The short piece functions as a quick differential-diagnosis tool for teachers trying to figure out which belief is actually driving a demotivated response.
points: Frames "when will I use this" as two overlapping problems — an inherited utilitarian worldview and an in-the-moment repulsion of the student's will — rather than a single simple complaint.
Argues the same surface complaint can stem from four different root causes (Credibility, Effort, Efficacy, or Belonging), each requiring a different fix before treating it as a Value problem.
Uses a garden-ecosystem metaphor to explain why the Five Key Beliefs can't be treated as independent on/off switches — they're interconnected and mutually reinforcing.
Positions Value-specific interventions (Mini-Sermons, Feasts of Knowledge, Valued Within) as a last resort, applied only once the other four beliefs have been ruled out as the actual cause.
quotes: This student's heart has been influenced at least a bit by the dominant utilitarian mentality that Westerners tend to bring to education: "If I can't see how what I'm learning is useful, then what I'm learning is a waste of time.
This student is genuinely struggling to WANT to do the work at hand. Something about it is repulsive to them — it is exerting a repulsive effect on their will.
As much as I wish student beliefs about my class were like little on/off switches, they act way more like different kinds of plants in a vibrant, interconnected garden ecosystem. They all connect.

These take time to improve — after all, as teachers we are in the counterculture business, and cultivating a counterculture isn't done in a day — but can slowly but steadily be helped through Mini-Sermons, Feasts of Knowledge, and Valued Within methods.
I wrote it because I wanted to address the common difficulties I encounter as a teacher, such as the difficulty I opened this article with.
